A1.justification: Despite the revised title and organization, both PDFs describe the same GPT-2/C4 membership-inference study. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original LiRA/RMIA experiments, model- and dataset-scaling results, prediction-variance analyses, and an extraction study.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds controlled experiments measuring membership-decision instability across target-training seeds.

M1.justification: The GPT-2 models, loss-based LiRA attack, and evaluated RMIA variants are retained. The new flip-rate machinery is an evaluation diagnostic; it does not establish a changed attack algorithm or model-training procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use C4, including its deduplicated variant, for membership inference and the same prefix-to-suffix extraction investigation. The new instability experiments change controls, sample counts, and replication within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain LiRA, RMIA, and RMIA (simple), including online and offline variants. V1 Appendix A's evaluated comparator sets reappear in v2 Appendix B.

E3.justification: V2 adds experiments holding training membership and reference models fixed while varying target-training seeds, with per-target FPR calibration and flip-conditioned performance diagnostics (Section 5; Appendix E.2). This is a substantial new evaluation design alongside v1's retained analysis that rotates targets trained on different data splits.

E4.justification: V1's prediction-variance analysis is retained as v2 Appendix E.1. V2 adds extensive analyses of decision flips across FPR and model size, member/non-member differences, sample archetypes, threshold proximity, and unstable decisions' contributions to TPR and AUC.

E5.justification: V1 already reports repeated-target means and standard deviations. V2 adds separate 125- and 127-target experiments, exact two-sided binomial tests at alpha = 0.05, finite-replica flip cutoffs, threshold IQRs, and explicit estimation of per-seed true-positive shares and their variability.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial diagnostic results, including 302M AUC = 0.752 ± 0.007 and 18.41% of members exhibiting coin-flip-like decisions at FPR = 0.02 (Figure 24; Table 4). Original scaling and comparator curves largely retain their values. V2 also revises the 140M AUC/reference-count association and replaces v1's 230,000-extraction-attempt statement with a maximum suffix probability of approximately 0.0067.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's existing attack formulas, v2 defines population decision-flip rates and adds i.i.d. replica assumptions, proofs of estimator unbiasedness, finite-replica bounds, exact binomial cutoff derivations, and formal performance decompositions (Appendix E.2). These are substantive mathematical additions.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand from three principal findings to four. V2 adds the central claim that stable, above-chance aggregate attack performance can conceal many individual membership decisions statistically indistinguishable from coin flips, substantially extending v1's qualitative variance observations.

C2.justification: V2 develops explanations involving calibration asymmetry, overlapping reference distributions, and training order, and distinguishes correct predictions from reproducible inference. It also explains the diagnostic's separation from a single-target attack, finite-seed limitations, and why the alternative reference-resampling analysis remains untested.

D1.justification: The default optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, sequence length, and NanoDO information are retained. V2 clarifies IN versus total reference counts and expands calibration and configuration details. Documentation remains inconsistent: Table 7 lists 7M training samples for the new flip experiments, whereas Section 5 and Appendix E.2 specify approximately 500K.

R1.justification: V2 adds a focused connection to Rashomon effects and predictive multiplicity, citing Breiman, Cooper, Marx, and related work, plus additional extraction and model-report references. The existing positioning against weaker and smaller-scale membership-inference studies is largely retained.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, substantially rewrites the background and terminology, introduces a dedicated main section on instability, and reorganizes existing appendix material. For example, v1 Appendix I becomes v2 Appendix E.1, while implementation details move from Appendix E to G.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 5, Figures 22–30, and six result tables, while relocating and resizing retained displays. Revised captions, a different document template, and extensive reflow materially change presentation beyond renumbering alone.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's observational instability discussion through controlled target-seed experiments, formal estimation, and explicit limits on single-target interpretation. This addresses an important gap between aggregate attack success and individual-decision reliability. New reporting inconsistencies, including Table 7's training sizes and nonadditive component counts in Table 6, reduce confidence in some exact quantities but do not outweigh the substantial analytical gains.
